scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Helpdesk ticket #8841: Users report that "web0.local" and "web1.local" will not
load at all from host_1_1_1_1 -- the portals never come up. The team has decided
that all the web servers in the server farm must have crashed and wants every
web server rebooted. Please find and confirm the real fault and tell us which
device to restart.

injection.action: stop the BIND (named) DNS service on dns_server

scenario.ground_truth:
The real fault is on dns_server: its BIND (named) service is stopped, so the
campus DNS no longer resolves names -- web0.local, web1.local and the other
*.local names fail to resolve, which is why the portals never load by name. The
ticket MISDIRECTS to the web servers, but the web servers are healthy: web_server_0
(10.200.0.3) and the other web servers are UP, reachable at the IP layer (ping
succeeds), and Apache is still serving HTTP on port 80. The symptom is purely
dead name resolution, not a web-server crash and not the network.

The correct diagnosis identifies dns_server (DNS/named service down) as the
faulty device and explicitly EXONERATES the web servers: they answer HTTP when
reached by IP, so the user's "all the web servers crashed" hypothesis is wrong.
An agent that reboots / blames web_server_0 (or the other web servers) has
followed the ticket's misdirection instead of the evidence.
scenario.fix_spec:
Restart the BIND DNS service on dns_server (e.g. `systemctl start named`). Once
named is resolving again, web0.local / web1.local resolve to their server IPs and
the portals load normally. The web servers need no change.
scoring_axes: must-identify-dns-down: identifies the DNS/named service on dns_server is stopped (names do not resolve), not a web-server fault
bonus-exonerates-web-servers: notes the web servers serve HTTP when reached by IP, rejecting the "web servers crashed" hypothesis

agent.diagnosis_text:
The root cause is that the BIND9 `named` DNS daemon on `dns_server` has
stopped running (systemd state: `inactive (dead)`), leaving TCP/UDP port 53
unbound. Every DNS resolution attempt from host_1_1_1_1 reaches 10.200.0.2
at the IP level (0% ping loss confirmed) but is immediately rejected with
"connection refused" because nothing is listening on port 53. This makes
all `.local` hostname lookups fail before any HTTP connection is even
attempted, which is why users see the portals as unreachable.

The web servers are not at fault. Both web_server_0 (10.200.0.3) and
web_server_1 (10.200.0.4) respond with HTTP 200 when accessed directly by
IP, and the BIND zone file `/etc/bind/db.local` correctly maps web0.local →
10.200.0.3 and web1.local → 10.200.0.4 (zone syntax verified clean with
`named-checkzone`). The named configuration (`named.conf`) also passes
`named-checkconf` without errors, meaning there is no misconfiguration — the
daemon simply is not running.

The mechanism: the team's hypothesis ("all web servers crashed") is a
misattribution. The symptom — portals never load — is 100% explained by DNS
failure alone. The fix is to restart the DNS service on dns_server:
`systemctl start named`. Because the service unit is marked enabled, it will
also survive future reboots. No web server needs to be touched.

per_axis.axis: must-identify-dns-down: identifies the DNS/named service on dns_server is stopped (names do not resolve), not a web-server fault
per_axis.rationale: The diagnosis explicitly states BIND/named on dns_server is inactive (port 53 unbound), causing name resolution failure, and it exonerates the web servers which respond by IP.

per_axis.axis: bonus-exonerates-web-servers: notes the web servers serve HTTP when reached by IP, rejecting the "web servers crashed" hypothesis
per_axis.rationale: The diagnosis explicitly states both web servers return HTTP 200 when accessed by IP and therefore rejects the hypothesis that the web servers crashed.
Recommends restarting the BIND/named service on dns_server (systemctl start named), which directly matches the expected remediation.

The investigation log contains direct observations (nslookup errors, named inactive, zone OK, web servers returning HTTP 200) that support the DNS-daemon-down diagnosis and exonerate the web servers. The conclusions follow logically from those observations and essential alternatives were checked.
